Hi! Is Mirsky's theorem in Mathlib? It's the order-dual of Dilworth. For a finite poset, the minimum number of antichains in a partition equals the longest chain length. I can't find it (no mirsky or dilworth in Mathlib), and I have a short proof (~180 lines) I'd like to PR as a new file Mathlib/Order/Mirsky.lean, importing only Mathlib.Order.Antichain and Mathlib.Order.Height. The main statement, in the Set/encard style of vertexCoverNum:

theorem isLeast_encard_antichainPartition {α : Type*} [PartialOrder α]
    {s : Set α} (hs : s.Finite) :
    IsLeast {n : ℕ∞ | ∃ 𝒜 : Set (Set α),
              (∀ A ∈ 𝒜, IsAntichain (· ≤ ·) A) ∧ 𝒜.PairwiseDisjoint id ∧
                ⋃₀ 𝒜 = s ∧ 𝒜.encard = n}
            (s.chainHeight (· < ·)) := by
  sorry

Would this be a welcome addition, and does the statement shape look right? (I used Set.chainHeight rather than Order.height, since the latter is edge-counted and whole-type.) Thanks!

Juan Pablo Silva Alvarado said:

no mirsky or dilworth in Mathlib

A proof of Dilworth's theorem exists in @Vlad Tsyrklevich's repo

Thanks @Snir Broshi , that's really helpful. I hadn't found that repo. @Vlad Tsyrklevich 's version is more complete than my independent Mirsky attempt (both theorems, a shared partition framework, and of course he wrote Set.chainHeight). @Vlad Tsyrklevich do you plan to upstream these to Mathlib? Happy to help with the PR legwork if that's useful, with you as author; otherwise I'd love to see them land.
One small thing I noticed comparing to my attempt: chainHeight/antichainWidth overlap Set.chainHeight from Order.Height, so a chunk of the supporting API could come for free by reusing it (unless the type-level version was deliberate). Minor, just stood out.

I wasn't planning to upstream it. There's an earlier thread with some thoughts you can find by searching for Dilworth. I'm not so well-informed on order theory but I think there are more general statements so I figured that's probably what belongs in mathlib unless there's some other theorem that we need it for. I was originally planning to also PR a similar Set.antichainWidth and then port my proof to the Set version but it's fallen off my list and I will not get to it. I came to think the Set version is better than using types, but I implemented it using types first.
